source: Klein, Calderwood, MacGregor (1989) Critical decision method for eliciting knowledge
finding: Founding paper of the Critical Decision Method (CDM). The expert retells one real, non-routine incident. The interviewer then sweeps through it several times with probes on cues, goals, options and what a novice would miss.
numbers: Cited 718 times (Crossref record). No effect sizes: it is a method paper.
limits: Original is paywalled and was NOT opened. Structure taken from open later sources (a03, a14, a16, a19).
agent_relevance: Template for our lessons: ask the agent to retell one hard past case, then probe the cues it used. Do not ask for abstract rules.

source: Klein (1991) Naturalistic Decision Making (HSIAC Gateway, vol 2 no 1)
finding: Describes the fireground work that led to CTA-style interviews. Fireground commanders said they did not compare options. They classed the situation, knew the typical action, and ran it in imagery to find flaws. This is the Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model. Searching for the optimal choice could stall them.
numbers: Coding of RPD studies reported with 87% to 94% inter-rater reliability. RPD applied to fireground, battle planning, critical care nursing, corporate information management, chess.
quote: They saw themselves as acting and reacting on the basis of prior experience
limits: Author's own summary. No sample sizes for the original fireground set in this text.
agent_relevance: What CTA finds first: experts act on recognised patterns, not option tables. Lessons built from CTA should hold cue-action patterns, not decision matrices.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox (Front Psychol)
finding: History of NDM from mid-1980s field studies to macrocognition and tools. States that RPD accounted for 80 to 90 percent of firefighter decisions, was replicated by other teams, and could not have been found in a lab because it rested on 10 to 20 years of experience. Cites a healthcare project that added CTA to find clinic decision styles.
numbers: RPD share 80-90% of firefighter decisions. Replications named: military leaders (Schmitt & Klein 1999), firefighters (Keren et al. 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998).
limits: Written by the model's author. The 80-90% is the authors' own coding, not a blind replication count.
agent_relevance: CTA output is a map of recognition, not a ranking of options. Check our lessons for this shape.

source: Hoffman, Crandall, Shadbolt (1998) Use of the Critical Decision Method to Elicit Expert Knowledge: A Case Study in the Methodology of CTA (Human Factors)
finding: Case study of CDM. Describes multiple-pass event retrospection guided by probe questions. Shows the outputs: situation assessment records, timelines, decision requirements. Also treats method questions such as reliability and validity of CTA.
numbers: Cited 297 times. Exact figures not recorded.
limits: Only the Crossref abstract was read; paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Output forms we could store as lessons: timelines and decision requirements.

source: Hoffman, Shadbolt, Burton, Klein (1995) Eliciting Knowledge from Experts: A Methodological Analysis (Org Behav Hum Decis Process)
finding: Methodological comparison of elicitation methods (unstructured and structured interviews, tasks, limited-information tasks) by efficiency and yield.
numbers: Cited 347 times (Crossref record). No figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Author list is from memory, not verified against the record.
agent_relevance: Basis for choosing the elicitation method by yield per hour.

source: Cooke (1994) Varieties of knowledge elicitation techniques (Int J Human-Computer Studies)
finding: Classic taxonomy of elicitation methods: observation, interviews, process tracing, conceptual methods. Later reviews build on it (see a23).
numbers: Cited 406 times (Crossref record).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Taxonomy to reuse when describing what our lesson builder asks for.

source: Nisbett & Wilson (1977) Telling more than we can know: Verbal reports on mental processes (Psychol Rev)
finding: Classic argument that people often cannot report the true causes of their judgments and give plausible theories instead. The main reason interview CTA anchors on concrete incidents, not opinions.
numbers: Cited 7382 times (Crossref record).
limits: Not opened. Ericsson & Simon argue reports are valid when concurrent and about attended content (not read here).
agent_relevance: Our agent's own self-explanations may be post-hoc stories. Test a self-reported cue with a counterfactual.

source: Sullivan, Yates, Inaba, Lam, Clark (2014) The use of CTA to reveal the instructional limitations of experts in the teaching of procedural skills (Acad Med)
finding: Three experts taught a cricothyrotomy on video, then did a CTA interview. They omitted most knowledge when teaching. Prompted CTA recovered a lot.
numbers: Omitted 71% (10/14) clinical knowledge steps, 51% (14/27) action steps, 73% (3.6/5) decision steps. Said 'how' for only 13% (3.6/27) of action steps. Steps described rose from 44% (20/46) unprompted to 66% (31/46) prompted. 3 experts, plus 3 surgeons for the gold list.
quote: experts unintentionally omit knowledge when describing a procedure
limits: Tiny sample, one procedure. The gold list was itself built by CTA, so partly circular. Abstract only (Europe PMC); full paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Free recall by an expert misses most decision steps. Our lesson builder should probe, not just ask for a summary.

source: Unaided recall vs simulation vs CTA, trauma surgeons (2012) The use of CTA to improve instructional descriptions of procedures (J Surg Res)
finding: Ten expert trauma surgeons described an emergency shunt. Three methods: unaided recall, recall with simulation, CTA. The CTA interview with one surgeon beat all unaided surgeons.
numbers: CTA about 70% more complete and accurate than free recall. Unaided surgeons omitted nearly 70% of decision steps. 4 free recall, 5 simulation, 1 CTA (random choice).
quote: CTA significantly increases the completeness and accuracy of surgeons' instructional descriptions
limits: N = 1 in the CTA arm. Authors not listed in the record read; likely the Clark lab (unverified). No independent replication found. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports a prompted protocol over a free summary. Weak causal evidence because N = 1.

source: Velmahos, Toutouzas, Sillin, Chan, Clark, Theodorou, Maupin (2004) CTA for teaching technical skills in an inanimate surgical skills laboratory (Am J Surg)
finding: Randomised trial. 26 interns got a 3-hour CTA-designed central venous catheter course or the usual route. The course group did better on test, checklist and attempts.
numbers: Repeat MCQ 11 +/- 1.86 vs 8.64 +/- 1.82 (P = 0.03). Checklist 12.6 vs 7.5 of 14 (P < 0.001). Attempts to find vein 3.3 vs 6.4 (P = 0.046). Time 15.4 vs 20.6 min (P = 0.149, not significant). Course n = 12, traditional n = 14.
limits: Control got no course, so CTA content is mixed with any extra training. Small N. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: CTA-built content helps novices, but the control is weak. We need an equal-time control lesson.

source: Tofel-Grehl & Feldon (2013) Cognitive Task Analysis-Based Training: A Meta-Analysis of Studies (J Cogn Eng Decis Mak)
finding: Compared CTA-based instruction with other ways of finding training content. Overall effect large, varies by CTA method and context.
numbers: Hedges g = 0.871 overall. Authors flag few studies.
quote: Overall, the effect of CTA-based instruction is large.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Small study count. Publication bias not reported in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Upper-end prior for how much a CTA-derived lesson might help. Expect less in our setting.

source: Cognitive task analysis-based training in surgery: a meta-analysis (BJS Open 2021)
finding: Systematic review. 2205 hits, 12 studies kept. Surgical trainees in CTA groups beat conventional training.
numbers: Knowledge SMD 1.36 (95% CI 0.67 to 2.05, P < 0.001). Technical performance SMD 2.06 (1.17 to 2.96). Heterogeneity I2 = 87% overall; 61% for trainee studies after removing a medical-student study; 60% in a subset. Risk of bias 'some concern'. Study quality moderate. Only seven studies documented the CTA method; all seven used more than one expert; three used modified Delphi.
limits: High heterogeneity. The medical-student study did not state its CTA method. Mostly simulated settings.
agent_relevance: CTA gains are real but noisy. Document the elicitation method; the undocumented one was the outlier.

source: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis: CTA vs conventional training for invasive medical procedures (J Surg Educ 2026)
finding: 15 RCTs found, 9 pooled. CTA improved procedural knowledge in surgical trainees but not in medical students.
numbers: Trainee knowledge SMD 2.08 (95% CI 1.46-2.71). All cognitive training: knowledge SMD 1.79 (1.45-2.14), technical SMD 1.73 (0.82-2.64).
limits: Abstract only. SMDs this large from small RCTs suggest small-study bias. No gain for learners without a base.
agent_relevance: Boundary: gains need a trainee with a base. An agent with no base skill may gain less.

source: Cognitive Task Analysis to Evaluate Resident Physician Decision Making in the ICU (ATS Scholar 2025)
finding: CDM interviews of third-year residents about real septic-shock fluid decisions, coded with the RPD model. Found cues, analogs and goals, plus misapplied volume heuristics and biases.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible residents completed a full interview. Median 7 days (IQR 6.5-11) from event to interview. Interviews 60-90 min. Seven domains: cues, information, decision making, alternatives, analogs, expected outcomes, goals. Residents assumed over 3-5 L meant no gain from more fluid. Biases: premature closure, confirmation, status quo.
limits: 48% completion. Retrospective, a week later. Self-report of bias. Descriptive, no outcome test.
agent_relevance: CDM can expose faulty heuristics in a learner, not only in experts. A CDM pass on our agent's failed runs could find its misapplied heuristics.

source: Use of cognitive task analysis in clinical and health services research: a systematic review (Pilot Feasibility Stud 2022)
finding: Methodological review of CTA for expert clinical decisions. CDM and CTA interviews dominate. Omission by experts is a named aim.
numbers: 81 articles (80 studies), 13 countries, 1993 to 2019. CDM n = 36, CTA interviews n = 30. Routine events n = 64, challenging n = 13, rare events n = 3. Training-model aim n = 14, tool-warranted aim n = 7.
limits: Methodological review. Quality of the CTA studies was not graded in the text read.
agent_relevance: Almost all CTA studies look at routine cases. Rare-event lessons are under-covered.

source: Klein & Borders (2016) The ShadowBox Approach to Cognitive Skills Training: An Empirical Evaluation (J Cogn Eng Decis Mak)
finding: ShadowBox turns CTA material into scenario training. Trainees rank options and write reasons, then see an expert panel's ranking and reasons. Match to experts rose with expert feedback.
numbers: Eval 1, Marines N = 59: Time 4 match .59 (SD .23) vs .44 (SD .24) no feedback, t(58) = 2.45, p = .02, d = .63, 28% better. Within feedback group .46 to .59, d = .51. Eval 2, soldiers N = 30, 1 hr tablet, .48 to .58, 21%, t(29) = -2.10, p = .04, d = .38, no control. Earlier fire officer study N = 29: 86.9 vs 73.6, F = 14.09, p < .001.
limits: Outcome is agreement with experts, not job performance. Eval 2 had no control. Authors evaluated their own method. With feedback 20 of 29 improved; without feedback 14 of 31 improved and 17 got worse (group sizes as printed; they sum to 60 vs N = 59).
agent_relevance: Direct model for a lesson: show a case, ask for ranked cues with reasons, then reveal the expert ranking and reasons. Measure the match.

source: Klein & Borders (2016) Good Stranger CTA study behind ShadowBox
finding: CTA interviews of people rated good at civilian encounters showed a trust-building sensemaking frame that weaker people lacked. The frame then drove the training scenarios.
numbers: 41 interviewees: 19 police officers and 22 military with overseas experience. Pilot of materials with 16 police officers.
limits: Selection by peer and supervisor ratings. The CTA report itself is a separate paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Contrast of skilled vs less skilled gives a frame, and the frame gives the lesson. Collect contrast pairs.

source: Klein & Borders (2016) note on probe types
finding: Action-based probes seemed weaker than cognitive and perceptual probes. With child protective caseworkers, skilled and journeyman workers differed sharply when asked about alternative priorities and which cues to monitor, not about which action to take.
numbers: Qualitative; cites Newsome, Wright, Klein, Flory, Baker (2015). No numbers in this passage.
quote: action-based probes may be less effective than other cognitive and perceptual probes
limits: Observation, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Probe cues and priorities, not the chosen action.

source: Wang, Zhang, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2023, v3 2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making
finding: CTA with four math teachers built a three-step decision model for answering student errors: infer error type, pick strategy, pick intention. Giving LLMs the expert decisions improved replies. Letting the LLM pick its own decisions also helped GPT-4 and Llama-2 but not GPT-3.5.
numbers: 700 real tutoring sessions. 12 model conditions plus expert; 40 response pairs per model; 3 blind Prolific teacher raters each. GPT-4 expert vs none: prefer +76%, useful +80%. Expert and self decisions 76-88% more preferred than none for GPT-4. Random decisions 67% worse than expert decisions. Experts up to 2.6x the no-decision models. Expert decisions did not raise 'care' for Llama-2 and GPT-3.5. Improvement significant at p < 0.05 two-tailed t-test for all models.
quote: Random decisions decrease GPT4's response quality -67% than expert decisions.
limits: Four experts, one domain, one country. Compared to original novice tutor replies, not learning outcomes. 40 pairs per model is small. Authors say the process compresses expert thought.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of CTA for LLM agents. A small structured decision model from CTA beat no structure. Random structure hurt, so content must fit the case.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Bridge: how the CTA was run
finding: Experts revised tutor replies. Weekly meetings used three questions: what did you notice, how did you want to react, why. Two teachers built the model, two others validated it. Options per step were refined until the experts and authors were satisfied with coverage.
numbers: 4 experts (3 female, 1 male); three with over 8 years teaching, one with 6. 11 strategies and 11 intentions in the final model. Pay $50/hour for building, $40/hour for annotating.
limits: Coverage judged by satisfaction, no reliability statistic.
agent_relevance: A cheap recipe: expert rewrites, then three probe questions. Reusable to turn our best runs into lessons.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Bridge: homogenisation of LLM decisions
finding: Expert decision paths were diverse. LLM self-chosen paths were narrow. GPT-3.5 mostly chose to correct the student directly.
numbers: Path entropy: expert 6.00, GPT-4 3.37. Random choice to force diversity was significantly worse than expert choice (p < 0.05 for GPT-4 and Llama-2).
limits: Entropy on test examples only; sample size not stated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Agents collapse onto one strategy. A lesson should widen the strategy set, chosen by cue and not at random.

source: Du, Jiang, Shen, Ren (2019) Eliciting Knowledge from Experts: Automatic Transcript Parsing for Cognitive Task Analysis
finding: Weakly supervised pipeline that turns CTA interview transcripts into flowchart-like structure: extract summary spans, then relations (next, if) between them, using human protocols as indirect supervision.
numbers: Best fuzzy matching 47.1% mention-level accuracy. Best sequence labelling 38.18% token-level accuracy. Best span-pair relation extraction 74.4% micro F1. Label sampling none:next:if = 4:2:1.
limits: BERT-era models, low-resource data. Low span accuracy means a human check is still needed. Not a modern LLM test.
agent_relevance: Transcript-to-procedure is the CTA bottleneck. Today an LLM could do it; measure it against human-parsed protocols.

source: Verostek, Griston et al. (2022) Making expert processes visible: how and why theorists use assumptions and analogies
finding: CTA-inspired interviews of theoretical physicists about one real project, coded as action, cue and sensemaking.
numbers: N = 11 physicists, five colleges. Five of 11 interviews coded with the main scheme: 663 actions, 326 sensemaking events, 472 cues. 128 assumption instances across all 11.
limits: Self-identified theorists, retrospective, small sample. Main coding on only five interviews.
agent_relevance: Action, cue, sensemaking is a ready coding frame for turning a reasoning trace into lesson parts.

source: Towards a criteria-based approach to selecting human-AI interaction mode (arXiv 2411.07406, 2024)
finding: Used ACTA-style interviews with a CDM deepening phase to score nine tasks for automation, augmentation or collaboration. CTA output (cognitive demands tables, flow diagrams) was the evidence for scoring.
numbers: Interviews: protein crystallisation N = 4, genome annotation N = 12, biological collections N = 8 (group). Nine tasks. Score clusters: 16 (one task), 24-30 (five), 35 (three). About 20% of scores were polar-opposite rater disagreements; another 15% medium vs low or high.
limits: Not a test of LLM performance. About 35% of scores needed resolution. Authors note CTA targets hard decision points and may miss easy but tedious tasks.
agent_relevance: CTA can pick which sub-tasks an agent should own. Expect rater disagreement when judging lessons.

source: A Multi-Disciplinary Review of Knowledge Acquisition Methods: From Human to Autonomous Eliciting Agents (arXiv 1802.09669, 2018)
finding: Classifies knowledge acquisition into human, human-inspired (automated interviews, protocol analysis) and autonomous agents. Lists CDM, simulation interview, protocol analysis, repertory grids. Says CDM is time consuming and needs a skilled elicitor.
numbers: Qualitative taxonomy. 'Big 3' stages: elicitation, interpretation, formalisation.
quote: The method is time consuming and requires elicitors to possess high level of expertise
limits: Review without effect sizes. Partly read (method sections).
agent_relevance: Places an LLM elicitor as a human-inspired agent doing interviews and protocol parsing.

source: Socially Interactive Agents for Preserving and Transferring Tacit Knowledge in Organizations (arXiv 2508.19942, 2025)
finding: Position paper. AI agents would interview employees to capture hard-to-state expertise. Raises privacy and trust concerns.
numbers: No measured results.
limits: Proposal only.
agent_relevance: An LLM as CTA interviewer is proposed but untested. A gap for us.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) fireground studies, as retold in Klein (1991)
finding: The studies that began this line: commanders interviewed about non-routine incidents. They matched the situation to a type and ran the first workable option in imagery. No option tables.
numbers: No counts in the 1991 text. The 80-90% RPD share comes from a03.
limits: 1986 report not opened. Counts are secondhand from the model's author.
agent_relevance: Base fact behind CTA: knowledge lives in cue patterns. Store a case library, not a rule list.

source: Gap check (this session): no LLM-as-CDM-interviewer study found
finding: arXiv search for 'critical decision method' gave 2 results, neither testing an LLM as interviewer. Search for 'cognitive task analysis' gave 13, and only Bridge (2023) tests LLM output using CTA-derived structure.
numbers: 2 and 13 results, arXiv title/abstract search, Nov 2026.
limits: Absence of evidence from a narrow search. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API were rate limited and the web search budget was spent. ACL, CHI and NDM venues not searched.
agent_relevance: Open chance: test an LLM running CDM sweeps on its own failed traces.
